heart_wall.name: Heart Wall (Myocardium)
heart_wall.description: The muscular outer wall of the heart. It encloses the four chambers (right and left atria, right and left ventricles) and contracts to pump blood. In this model the chambers are part of one wall mesh; turn on X-ray to see the valves and papillary muscles inside.
facts: The wall has three layers: epicardium (outer), myocardium (muscle) and endocardium (inner lining).
The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood to the whole body.
Heart muscle (cardiac muscle) contracts on its own rhythm, set by the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium.
An adult heart is roughly the size of a closed fist and usually weighs about 250-350 g.

aorta.name: Aorta
aorta.description: The body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the rest of the body.
facts: Has three sections shown here: the ascending aorta, the aortic arch and the descending aorta.
The aortic arch gives off branches that supply the head and arms.
The coronary arteries branch from its root, just above the aortic valve.
In adults it is roughly 2.5-3 cm wide near the heart.

pulmonary_artery.name: Pulmonary Artery
pulmonary_artery.description: Carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The trunk splits into right and left pulmonary arteries.
facts: One of the few arteries that carries oxygen-poor blood.
Begins at the pulmonary valve.
Shown in blue here by the common teaching convention for oxygen-poor blood.
High blood pressure in these vessels is called pulmonary hypertension.

pulmonary_veins.name: Pulmonary Veins
pulmonary_veins.description: Veins that carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the left atrium.
facts: There are usually four: two from each lung.
They are the only veins in adults that carry oxygen-rich blood.
Shown in red here because they carry oxygen-rich blood.

superior_vena_cava.name: Superior Vena Cava
superior_vena_cava.description: Large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium.
facts: Formed where the left and right brachiocephalic veins join.
Has no valve where it enters the right atrium.
Drains blood from the upper half of the body.

inferior_vena_cava.name: Inferior Vena Cava
inferior_vena_cava.description: The largest vein in the body; it returns oxygen-poor blood from the legs, abdomen and pelvis to the right atrium.
facts: Runs up the abdomen to the right of the aorta.
Passes through the diaphragm before entering the right atrium.
Only the part near the heart is shown here.

tricuspid_valve.name: Tricuspid Valve
tricuspid_valve.description: Valve between the right atrium and right ventricle that stops blood flowing back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
facts: Usually has three leaflets (cusps), which gives it its name.
Its leaflets are held by chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles.
It is an atrioventricular (AV) valve, like the mitral valve.

mitral_valve.name: Mitral Valve
mitral_valve.description: Valve between the left atrium and left ventricle. It opens to let blood into the left ventricle and closes to stop it flowing back when the ventricle contracts.
facts: Has two leaflets, so it is also called the bicuspid valve.
Named after a bishop's mitre because of its shape.
Its closing is part of the first heart sound ('lub').
In mitral valve prolapse the leaflets bulge back into the atrium.

pulmonary_valve.name: Pulmonary Valve
pulmonary_valve.description: Valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery that lets blood out to the lungs and stops it flowing back.
facts: Has three semilunar cusps.
Its closing contributes to the second heart sound ('dub').
It works at lower pressure than the aortic valve.

right_coronary_artery.name: Right Coronary Artery
right_coronary_artery.description: Artery that runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle and supplies blood to the right side of the heart muscle.
facts: Branches from the right side of the aortic root.
Its branches shown here include the marginal branch and the posterior interventricular branch.
In most people it supplies the sinoatrial (SA) node.
Blockage can cause a heart attack affecting the lower (inferior) wall of the heart.

left_coronary_artery.name: Left Coronary Artery
left_coronary_artery.description: Artery that supplies most of the left side of the heart muscle. A short stem splits into the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex branches.
facts: Branches from the left side of the aortic root.
The anterior interventricular branch is often called the LAD (left anterior descending) artery.
The circumflex branch curves around the left side of the heart.
A blockage of the LAD is a common cause of serious heart attacks.

cardiac_veins.name: Cardiac Veins
cardiac_veins.description: Veins on the heart's surface that collect oxygen-poor blood from the heart muscle.
facts: Includes the great, middle and anterior cardiac veins and the posterior veins of the left ventricle.
Most drain into the coronary sinus.
The anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium.

coronary_sinus.name: Coronary Sinus
coronary_sinus.description: A wide vein on the back of the heart that collects blood from most cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium.
facts: Lies in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle on the back of the heart.
Opens into the right atrium.
Doctors use it as a route for some pacemaker leads.

papillary_muscles.name: Papillary Muscles
papillary_muscles.description: Small muscles inside the ventricles that anchor the tricuspid and mitral valve leaflets through cords (chordae tendineae).
facts: The right ventricle has three (anterior, posterior and septal); the left ventricle has two.
They contract with the ventricle to stop the valve leaflets flipping back into the atria.
Turn on X-ray to see them inside the heart wall.
